    Comparing segmentations¶

    This tutorial aims to show how testing multiple segmentation methods (e.g. Cellpose/Proseg/Baysor/Comseg) or different set of segmentation parameters to compare them and find the best segmentation.

    We will run three segmentations, and compare them: Cellpose with two sets of parameters, and also Baysor.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import spatialdata

import sopa
    import spatialdata import sopa

    As usual, we will show this example on a toy dataset.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    sdata_full = sopa.io.toy_dataset()
    sdata_full = sopa.io.toy_dataset()
    [INFO] (sopa.utils.data) Image of size (4, 2048, 2048) with 400 cells and 100 transcripts per cell

    Cropping your data¶

    This step is optional, although recommended. Indeed, cropping the data allows to quickly run multiple segmentation methods with multiple parameters, and compare them. Afterwards, you can keep the best segmentation method/parameters, and run it on the full dataset.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    sdata_full
    sdata_full
    Out[4]:
    SpatialData object
├── Images
│     ├── 'he_image': DataTree[cyx] (3, 1024, 1024), (3, 512, 512), (3, 256, 256)
│     └── 'image': DataArray[cyx] (4, 2048, 2048)
├── Points
│     └── 'transcripts': DataFrame with shape: (<Delayed>, 5) (2D points)
└── Shapes
      └── 'cells': GeoDataFrame shape: (400, 1) (2D shapes)
with coordinate systems:
    ▸ 'global', with elements:
        he_image (Images), image (Images), transcripts (Points), cells (Shapes)
    ▸ 'microns', with elements:
        transcripts (Points)

    Here, we subset our sdata_full object based on a bounding from of width 1000 pixels. You can look at the above coordinates to choose an appropriate bounding box.

    Then, we save this crop as a new .zarr directory.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    sdata = sdata_full.query.bounding_box(
    axes=["y", "x"], min_coordinate=[0, 0], max_coordinate=[1000, 1000], target_coordinate_system="global"
)

sdata.write("subset.zarr")
sdata = spatialdata.read_zarr("subset.zarr")  # read the data from the zarr directory
    sdata = sdata_full.query.bounding_box( axes=["y", "x"], min_coordinate=[0, 0], max_coordinate=[1000, 1000], target_coordinate_system="global" ) sdata.write("subset.zarr") sdata = spatialdata.read_zarr("subset.zarr") # read the data from the zarr directory

    Creating the patches¶

    As usual, we create the patches for the segmentation.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    sopa.make_image_patches(sdata)
sopa.make_transcript_patches(sdata)
    sopa.make_image_patches(sdata) sopa.make_transcript_patches(sdata)
    [INFO] (sopa.patches.patches) Added 1 patch(es) to sdata['image_patches']

    [########################################] | 100% Completed | 105.65 ms

    [INFO] (sopa.patches.transcripts) Added 1 patch(es) to sdata['transcripts_patches']

    Running multiple segmentations¶

    We run three segmentations:

    • Cellpose on DAPI only, with diameter=35
    • Cellpose on CK and DAPI, with diameter=15
    • Baysor, with scale=2 microns (expected cell radius).

    Note that we use key_added to precise the name that we want to give to each segmentation.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    sopa.segmentation.cellpose(sdata, "DAPI", diameter=35, key_added="cellpose_DAPI_35")

sopa.segmentation.cellpose(sdata, ["CK", "DAPI"], diameter=15, key_added="cellpose_CK_DAPI_15")

sopa.segmentation.baysor(sdata, scale=2, key_added="baysor_scale_2")
    sopa.segmentation.cellpose(sdata, "DAPI", diameter=35, key_added="cellpose_DAPI_35") sopa.segmentation.cellpose(sdata, ["CK", "DAPI"], diameter=15, key_added="cellpose_CK_DAPI_15") sopa.segmentation.baysor(sdata, scale=2, key_added="baysor_scale_2")

    Now, inside the shapes, with all our three segmentations: 'cellpose_DAPI_35', 'cellpose_CK_DAPI_15', and 'baysor_scale_2'.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    list(sdata.shapes.keys())
    list(sdata.shapes.keys())
    Out[8]:
    ['cells',
 'image_patches',
 'transcripts_patches',
 'cellpose_DAPI_35',
 'cellpose_CK_DAPI_15',
 'baysor_scale_2']

    Then, we can aggregate the transcripts inside the cells. Since we have multiple shapes layers, we need to precise shapes_key.

    Also, we can set a specific name for the table that will be created (via key_added), or keep key_added=None which will use the name "{shapes_key}_table" by default.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    sopa.aggregate(sdata, shapes_key="cellpose_DAPI_35", key_added=None)
sopa.aggregate(sdata, shapes_key="cellpose_CK_DAPI_15", key_added=None)
sopa.aggregate(sdata, shapes_key="baysor_scale_2", key_added=None)
    sopa.aggregate(sdata, shapes_key="cellpose_DAPI_35", key_added=None) sopa.aggregate(sdata, shapes_key="cellpose_CK_DAPI_15", key_added=None) sopa.aggregate(sdata, shapes_key="baysor_scale_2", key_added=None)

    Now, we have one table for each shape layer:

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    list(sdata.tables.keys())
    list(sdata.tables.keys())
    Out[10]:
    ['table',
 'cellpose_DAPI_35_table',
 'cellpose_CK_DAPI_15_table',
 'baysor_scale_2_table']

    Comparison¶

    Now, we can compare the different shapes / tables to see which segmentation method or which parameters were the best. We show some simple analysis below that can help us decide between the three.

    Feel free to perform more sophisticated quality checks.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    # the different table names that were created
table_names = ["cellpose_DAPI_35_table", "cellpose_CK_DAPI_15_table", "baysor_scale_2_table"]
    # the different table names that were created table_names = ["cellpose_DAPI_35_table", "cellpose_CK_DAPI_15_table", "baysor_scale_2_table"]

    Visual comparison¶

    We can plot the images / shapes / transcripts to visually find the best segmentation. Here, we can definitely see that "cellpose_DAPI_CK_15" is not good, as the cells are very small. It appears that diameter=15 was not a good Cellpose parameter for this image.

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    import spatialdata_plot
    import spatialdata_plot
    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    # Cellpose on DAPI with diameter 35
sdata.pl.render_images("image").pl.render_shapes(
    "cellpose_DAPI_35", fill_alpha=0, outline_color="#FFFFFF", outline_alpha=1
).pl.show("global")

# Cellpose on DAPI and CK with diameter 15
sdata.pl.render_images("image").pl.render_shapes(
    "cellpose_CK_DAPI_15", fill_alpha=0, outline_color="#FFFFFF", outline_alpha=1
).pl.show("global")

# Baysor with scale 2
sdata.pl.render_images("image").pl.render_shapes(
    "baysor_scale_2", fill_alpha=0, outline_color="#FFFFFF", outline_alpha=1
).pl.show("global")
    # Cellpose on DAPI with diameter 35 sdata.pl.render_images("image").pl.render_shapes( "cellpose_DAPI_35", fill_alpha=0, outline_color="#FFFFFF", outline_alpha=1 ).pl.show("global") # Cellpose on DAPI and CK with diameter 15 sdata.pl.render_images("image").pl.render_shapes( "cellpose_CK_DAPI_15", fill_alpha=0, outline_color="#FFFFFF", outline_alpha=1 ).pl.show("global") # Baysor with scale 2 sdata.pl.render_images("image").pl.render_shapes( "baysor_scale_2", fill_alpha=0, outline_color="#FFFFFF", outline_alpha=1 ).pl.show("global")

    Tables comparison¶

    We can also compute some simple quality controls, such as the mean transcript count per cell, or the distribution of transcript count. Again, we see that cellpose with diameter=15 was worse than the two other segmentations.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns
    In [15]:
    Copied! 
    for name in table_names:
    adata = sdata.tables[name]
    n_cells = adata.n_obs
    total_count = adata.X.sum()
    transcript_counts = adata.X.sum(axis=1).A1
    mean_count_per_cell = transcript_counts.mean()

    print(f"Table: {name}, {n_cells=}, {total_count=}, {mean_count_per_cell=:.2f}")
    sns.displot(transcript_counts, kde=True)
    plt.title("Distribution of transcript counts per cell")
    plt.show()
    for name in table_names: adata = sdata.tables[name] n_cells = adata.n_obs total_count = adata.X.sum() transcript_counts = adata.X.sum(axis=1).A1 mean_count_per_cell = transcript_counts.mean() print(f"Table: {name}, {n_cells=}, {total_count=}, {mean_count_per_cell=:.2f}") sns.displot(transcript_counts, kde=True) plt.title("Distribution of transcript counts per cell") plt.show()
    Table: cellpose_DAPI_35_table, n_cells=95, total_count=np.int64(9512), mean_count_per_cell=100.13

    Table: cellpose_CK_DAPI_15_table, n_cells=188, total_count=np.int64(8445), mean_count_per_cell=44.92

    Table: baysor_scale_2_table, n_cells=96, total_count=np.int64(9564), mean_count_per_cell=99.62

    UMAP comparisons¶

    We can also compute a UMAP on all tables, and look which table gives the best separation. Here, it seems that Baysor is slightly cleaner.

    In [16]:
    Copied! 
    import scanpy as sc
    import scanpy as sc
    In [17]:
    Copied! 
    for name in table_names:
    adata = sdata.tables[name]
    sc.pp.normalize_total(adata)
    sc.pp.log1p(adata)
    sc.pp.neighbors(adata)
    sc.tl.umap(adata)
    sc.tl.leiden(adata, flavor="igraph")

    sc.pl.umap(adata, color="leiden")
    plt.show()
    for name in table_names: adata = sdata.tables[name] sc.pp.normalize_total(adata) sc.pp.log1p(adata) sc.pp.neighbors(adata) sc.tl.umap(adata) sc.tl.leiden(adata, flavor="igraph") sc.pl.umap(adata, color="leiden") plt.show()

    Next steps¶

    After the above comparison, you should have found the right method / parameters for your dataset.

    You can now use these parameters to run Sopa on the full slide or cohort. For that, refer to the other tutorials, for instance the API or Snakemake tutorials.
